newsitem.title: USA: AT&T's Walter planning management shake-up.
newsitem.headline: AT&T's Walter planning management shake-up.

text.p: AT&T Corp. chief operating officer John Walter is scrapping the company's plan to regionalize consumer and small business marketing and sales and may eliminate an entire layer of management.

Two sources close to the company say Walter's first shake-up of AT&T management will reverse a move to spread many hundreds of marketing and sales staff among offices in Chicago, New York, Atlanta and Basking Ridge, N.J.
"There will be job cuts, and those will be explained as part of the process begun in 1996," said one source.

Walter is also looking at removing one of the four tiers of management beneath vice president level, and may introduce a new package of incentives to persuade some longer-serving managers to leave early, one source said.
Analysts and industry sources say that Walter needs to show he is in charge well before he formally takes over from Robert Allen as chief executive, slated for May 1998.
"The new structure will be announced in March, which makes sense as that is when Walter meets analysts," the source said.
AT&T declined to comment on the regionalization plan or the changes in management structure, but acknowledged a thorough review was under way.
"Under John Walter's leadership all areas of the business are being looked at. In my 17 years at AT&T I have never seen anything like it," said Mark Siegel, an AT&T spokesman.
AT&T in January last year said 40,000 jobs would go as part of its split into three firms.
The telecommunications firm, which retained the AT&T name after the split became effective at the end of last year, said it has so far cut 5,700 of the 17,000 to be cut by end-1998.
Those job cuts are not net reductions in overall AT&T employment and may be partially offset by new jobs in growing areas within the company like Internet services, AT&T says.

Investors have taken a jaundiced view of AT&T in the last year of so, selling the stock on worries about increasing competition, executive departures and the management succession to chief executive and chairman Robert Allen.
Allen is expected to return to work by the end of the month after surgery last week to correct a heart valve.
He has been criticised by some analysts for failing to tackle AT&T's problems, for picking a relative unknown, Walter, as his successor and for making the succession too slow.
Walter was recruited from printing firm R.R. Donnelley & Sons Co. which, as chief executive, he had turned around.

Since the start of 1996, AT&T stock, adjusted for spin offs of Lucent Technologies Inc. and NCR Corp. has fallen more than 25 percent, while the S&P 500 index has risen more than 30 percent in the same period.
However, Siegel denied reports that a deep round of job cuts was being put in place that would be larger than envisaged in the 1996 plan.
"That is categorically untrue," he said.
Sources close to the company said Walter was looking particularly hard at management, with a view to removing whole structures rather than just trimming them back.
"They (managers) are all basically reapplying for their old jobs," one source said, adding that Walter was nevertheless making a favourable impression on his extensive rounds to meet employees.
"He is meeting many people within the organisation and those that meet him are impressed, but he needs to meet many more," he said.
((-- New York Newsrom 212 859 1610))
